$comment: FAA ORDER 5300.7 GEAR CONFIGURATIONS.
Sixteen configurations from the standard naming convention, as loadable
models. Every one of them is SCHEMATIC and says so — `kind: "schematic"`,
an amber notice in the panel and a flag in the title block. They exist to
show what a gear NAME means, which is a different job from modelling an
aircraft, and the distinction is worth keeping sharp: a reader who mistook
one of these for a measured aircraft would be taking a nominal wheelbase
and a nominal tire size for published figures.
WHAT IS REAL HERE, AND WHAT IS NOT.
REAL, and cited per gear: the LATERAL AND LONGITUDINAL WHEEL GEOMETRY of
every configuration whose representative aircraft appears in the FAARFIELD
2.1.1 aircraft library — track, dual spacing, tandem spacing, body-gear
offset, and the uneven bogies that a single spacing cannot express. That
library publishes per-wheel coordinates in millimetres and is the same
source this project already relies on to corroborate the 747 and the A380
(see airbus.json). Ten of the sixteen are sourced this way.
NOMINAL, and declared in assumedFields on every unit:
- THE TIRE. FAARFIELD carries a contact patch and an inflation pressure,
not a Tire and Rim Association designation, and no other consulted
source gives one for these aircraft. The tire is therefore a stand-in,
chosen to fit the real spacings; it sets how large the rendered wheel
is and nothing else. It does not move a single wheel centre.
- THE WHEELBASE. FAARFIELD models the main gear only, because the nose
gear carries too little load to matter to pavement thickness design.
The nose gear's TYPE is real — Table 3 tabulates it in its own column —
but its distance forward is nominal.
THE SIX PURE PATTERNS. `T`, `Q`, `2Q`, `3S`, `3T` and `3Q` are Figure 2
configurations with no aircraft behind them, or none whose geometry any
consulted source publishes. They are drawn to ONE nominal scale so that the
twelve cells of Figure 2 stay comparable, which is the whole point of that
figure: 49x19.0-22 tires, 1400 mm lateral pitch, 1450 mm longitudinal pitch,
strut centres 1800 mm outboard of the bogie's own half-width, dual nose gear
at 900 mm, wheelbase 20 000 mm. Not one of those numbers describes an
aircraft. They are the drawing's scale, and they are stated here so that a
reader can see they were chosen rather than measured.
NO OUTER WIDTH IS STATED, and that is deliberate. On the real aircraft in
this library the FAA's published main gear outer width is the load-bearing
datum and the track is derived from it. Here the relationship runs the
other way: the track is measured and the outer width would depend on the
NOMINAL tire, so stating one would dress a placeholder up as a datum.
`mainGearOuterWidth` is null on every unit in this file and the validator's
closure check correctly skips it.
WHAT IS NOT HERE. Five of Table 3's codes — D, 2D, 3D, 2D/2D2 and 2D/3D2 —
already have fully sourced aircraft in this library (737-800, 757-200 and
767-400ER, 777-300ER, 747-400 and 747-8, A380-800). The catalogue points at
those rather than duplicating them with a schematic, because a measured
aircraft is strictly better than a drawing of one.

units.notes: Eight wheels on two struts, all in one line across. Table 3 names the HS-121 Trident, an aircraft out of service since 1985 — which is why this configuration's geometry is nominal while most of its neighbours' are measured. Four wheels on a single axle line is a rare arrangement: heavy aircraft almost always reach the same wheel count by going tandem instead, because that spreads the load along the pavement rather than concentrating it across one transverse line.

Neither shows at the scale a gear diagram is read at, and both are in the FAARFIELD coordinates if you need them.

gears.source: Nose gear TYPE is dual wheel, from FAA Order 5300.7 Table 3, the Figure 10 row. Position, spacing and tire nominal.

WING gear. Strut centreline 5334.0 mm and dual spacing 1371.6 mm from the FAARFIELD 2.1.1 wheel coordinates for the DC10-30/40 (X ±4648.2 and ±6019.8 mm); tandem spacing 1625.6 mm from the same source (Y -50.8 and +1574.8 mm). Longitudinal position follows from the nominal wheelbase and the sourced 762.0 mm offset to the body gear. Tire nominal.
Mirror of WLG-L about the aircraft centreline; same derivation.

BODY gear, on the aircraft centreline: a single dual-wheel axle, and the reason the designation carries a /D1 rather than stopping at 2D. Dual spacing 952.5 mm from the FAARFIELD 2.1.1 'DC10-30/40 Belly' entry (X ±476.25 mm), which also places it 762.0 mm AFT of the wing bogie centre. THE DIRECTION OF THIS OFFSET IS CORROBORATED INDEPENDENTLY. FAARFIELD stores an aircraft and its 'Belly' entry on a SHARED longitudinal datum whose origin is the body gear, with positive Y forward. The proof is the 747-400: its FAARFIELD wing gear sits at Y 3073.4 mm, and Boeing's own ACAP section 7.2.1 footprint figure - read separately, for boeing.json in this same library - puts the 747 body gear 3073 mm AFT of the wing gear. The two agree to 0.4 mm from wholly independent documents, which fixes both the datum and the sign. Tire nominal.

units.notes: The configuration Order 5300.7 §3a uses to introduce the whole problem: Douglas built the DC-10 with two dual-tandem struts, then added a centreline strut for the heavier -30, and the old three-name vocabulary had nowhere to put it. Note the body-gear count is written even though there is only one — §6f keeps it because a body gear may be asymmetric, so 2D/D and 2D/D1 could not be allowed to mean the same thing. FAARFIELD apportions 78 % of the aircraft weight to the two wing struts and 17 % to the body gear, which is NOT an equal share per tire; this model uses the equal split that the 95 % main-gear figure implies, so its per-tire loads are nominal even though its geometry is not.

The proof is the 747-400: its FAARFIELD wing gear sits at Y 3073.4 mm, and Boeing's own ACAP section 7.2.1 footprint figure - read separately, for boeing.json in this same library - puts the 747 body gear 3073 mm AFT of the wing gear. The stated wheelbase is the tire-weighted centroid of all twelve main tires, so it sits aft of the wing bogie: the body gear pulls it 580 mm back. FAARFIELD apportions 72 % of the weight to the wing struts and 23 % to the body gear; this model uses the equal per-tire split, so its loads are nominal and its geometry is not.

units.notes: Twenty main wheels in two files of five. Order 5300.7 §6h explains the choice of name: the An-124 physically has five separate landing struts per side, so D5 — dual wheels, five gears in line — would also describe it, but 'it is more advantageous to address the multiple landing struts as one gear, i.e. 5D or five duals in tandem'. Compare the IL-76, where the Order goes the other way and uses Q2 precisely because its struts are far enough apart to read as separate gears. The distinction is proximity, and it is a judgement the Order makes explicitly rather than leaving to the reader.

units.notes: The one configuration Order 5300.7 refuses to name by its own convention. §6h: 'The Lockheed C-5 Galaxy has a unique gear type and is difficult to name using the proposed method. This aircraft will not be classified using the new naming convention and will continue to be referred to directly as the C5.' The reason is visible in the model: each of its four bogies carries a quadruple axle AND a dual axle, so no single gear code fits — the code assumes every axle line on a strut is the same width. Twenty-four main wheels in all. This app therefore models it as eight axles rather than four bogies, which is the only honest way to express a mixed bogie in a schema built on wheels-across times rows.

units.notes: The only bicycle gear in the Order and the only configuration here with NO NOSE GEAR: two struts fore and two aft, carrying the aircraft between them, with a single outrigger wheel under each wingtip. Figure 18's caption says those outriggers are ignored, which is why the wheel count is 8 and not 10. Two consequences follow and both are visible in this model. There is no wheelbase — the quantity is defined from the nose gear, and there is none, so it is null rather than invented. And percentOnMainGear is null too: the 95 % design figure exists to split load between nose and main gear, and with the outriggers disregarded this aircraft's entire weight is on the main gear. FAARFIELD apportions it 52 % forward and 48 % aft.

units.notes: Sixteen main wheels, four across on each of four struts. Order 5300.7 §6h pairs this aircraft with the An-124 to show where the line falls: both have several struts per side, but 'in contrast the IL-76 has considerable spacing between the struts and should be designated as a Q2', whereas the An-124's are close enough to be read as one five-axle gear. The two names encode the same judgement a pavement engineer would make by eye — do these wheels load the pavement as one group or as two?
